overview.title: Finishing the subclassed ticket model; Layer vs Model; training it
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: The rest of CustomerTicketModel.call(), instantiating the model and creating its weights by calling it on data, the difference between a Layer subclass and a Model subclass, and compiling and fitting the subclassed model with structures that match what call() expects and returns.
overview.central_idea: A subclassed model creates its weights the first time it is called on data. It differs from a Layer mainly in being the top-level object you train and export: it has fit(), evaluate() and predict() (and can be saved). It is compiled and trained like any other model, but the structure of the losses, metrics, inputs and targets must match exactly what call() consumes and returns.
overview.importance: The structure-matching rule is the practical key to training subclassed models (there are no named output layers to key on), and the Layer vs Model distinction clarifies when to subclass which.
learning_objectives: Trace the forward pass of CustomerTicketModel.call() line by line.
Explain when a subclassed model creates its weights.
State the difference between a Layer subclass and a Model subclass.
Compile and fit a subclassed model with loss/metric/target structures that match call()'s return value and input structures that match what call() reads.
prerequisites: List- and dict-based training of the Functional ticket model (p.222-223)

summary:
The page completes **Listing 7.14**. After reading `title` (p.226), `call()` reads `text_body = inputs["text_body"]` and `tags = inputs["tags"]`. It then computes `features = self.concat_layer([title, text_body, tags])` and `features = self.mixing_layer(features)`, applies the two heads (`priority = self.priority_scorer(features)`, `department = self.department_classifier(features)`), and ends with `return priority, department`. This is exactly the computation of the Functional model of Listing 7.9, written as imperative code.

The model is instantiated with `model = CustomerTicketModel(num_departments=4)`. The authors note that it only creates its weights the first time you call it on some data, much like `Layer` subclasses. The example calls it on the dict `{"title": title_data, "text_body": text_body_data, "tags": tags_data}` and gets `priority, department`.

What distinguishes a `Layer` subclass from a `Model` subclass? A **layer** is a building block you use to create models; a **model** is the top-level object that you actually train, export for inference, and so on. In short, a `Model` has `fit()`, `evaluate()` and `predict()`; layers don't. Otherwise the two classes are "virtually identical," except that a model can also be saved to a file on disk, which is covered a few sections later.

Finally, the subclassed model is compiled and trained like a Sequential or Functional model: `loss=["mean_squared_error", "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"]`, `metrics=[["mean_absolute_error"], ["accuracy"]]`, and `fit()` with a dict of inputs and a list `[priority_data, department_data]` of targets for one epoch. The two callouts state the rule. The structure of loss and metrics must match exactly what `call()` returns (two elements, so lists of two). The input data must match what `call()` expects (a dict with keys `title`, `text_body`, `tags`), and the target data must match what it returns (a list of two elements).

concepts.name: Model subclassing
concepts.definition: Defining a model by subclassing keras.Model with layers in __init__() and the forward pass in call().
concepts.intuition: The model is a Python program.
concepts.technical: Weights are created on first call; compile/fit/evaluate/predict work as usual; output structure is whatever call() returns.
concepts.significance: Maximum flexibility; the trade-offs are discussed on p.228.
concepts.misconception: That subclassed models need custom training loops.

concepts.name: Layer vs Model
concepts.definition: A layer is a building block for models; a model is the top-level object you train and export.
concepts.intuition: Bricks vs the finished building you use.
concepts.technical: Model adds fit(), evaluate(), predict() and saving to disk; otherwise the classes are virtually identical.
concepts.example: A custom attention block would be a Layer; the classifier containing it, a Model.
concepts.misconception: That models cannot be used as layers inside other models; they can (p.228).

concepts.name: Structure matching for training
concepts.definition: Loss, metrics and targets must have the same structure as call()'s return value; inputs must have the structure call() expects.
concepts.intuition: Each answer key must line up with an answer the model gives.
concepts.technical: call() returns two tensors, so loss and metrics are lists of two and targets a list of two; call() reads dict keys, so x is a dict with title, text_body, tags.
concepts.significance: Without named output layers, positional structure is how Keras pairs targets with outputs.
concepts.misconception: That you can key the targets by "priority"/"department" as with the Functional model; those names were output layer names there, and the subclassed model returns an unnamed pair.

        tags = inputs["tags"]

code.title: Compiling and training the subclassed model
code.original_code:
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=["mean_squared_error", "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"],
    metrics=[["mean_absolute_error"], ["accuracy"]],
)
model.fit(
    {"title": title_data, "text_body": text_body_data, "tags": tags_data},
    [priority_data, department_data],
    epochs=1,
)

Callout: inputs must match what call() expects (a dict with title, text_body, tags); targets must match what call() returns (a list of two elements).

code.theory_link: Subclassed models use the same training APIs as Sequential and Functional models.

deeper.title: Three models, one computation
deeper.body:
| | Functional (p.221-223) | Subclassed (p.226-227) |
|---|---|---|
| inputs declared | `keras.Input(shape=..., name=...)` | dict keys read in `call()` |
| wiring | stored graph | Python code in `call()` |
| weights created | when layers are called on Inputs | on first call on real data |
| targets/losses | list or dict by output name | structure of `call()`'s return |
| plot/feature extraction | yes | no (p.228) |

deeper.title: Why structure matching replaces names
deeper.body:
1. `call()` returns `(priority, department)`.
2. Keras flattens this to output 0 and output 1.
3. `loss[0]` and `metrics[0]` are paired with output 0, `loss[1]` and `metrics[1]` with output 1.
4. In `fit`, `y[0]` is compared with output 0 and `y[1]` with output 1.

If `call()` returned a dict such as `{"priority": ..., "department": ...}`, then dicts keyed by those names would be the matching structure (beyond the book).

misconceptions.claim: A Model subclass needs its own training loop.
misconceptions.correction: It is compiled and trained with compile() and fit() like Sequential and Functional models.

misconceptions.claim: Layer and Model subclasses are fundamentally different.
misconceptions.correction: They are virtually identical; a Model adds fit(), evaluate(), predict() and saving to disk.

misconceptions.claim: The subclassed model has weights as soon as it is instantiated.
misconceptions.correction: Weights are created the first time it is called on data.

takeaways: call() of CustomerTicketModel reproduces the Functional ticket model's computation and returns (priority, department).
Subclassed models create their weights on the first call on data.
Layer = building block; Model = top-level object with fit(), evaluate(), predict() and saving.
Subclassed models are compiled and trained like any other model.
Loss, metrics and targets must match call()'s output structure; inputs must match what call() expects.

questions.question: When does CustomerTicketModel create its weights?
options: The first time the model is called on data
questions.answer: The first time the model is called on data
questions.explanation: The page says it only creates its weights the first time you call it on some data, like Layer subclasses. At definition or instantiation input shapes are unknown; compile() does not build weights.

questions.question: According to the book, what is the difference between a Layer and a Model?
questions.answer: A layer is a building block for creating models; a model is the top-level object you train and export. A Model has fit(), evaluate() and predict() (and can be saved to disk); layers don't. Otherwise they are virtually identical.

questions.question: Why must the targets in fit() be a list of two elements for the subclassed model?
questions.answer: Because call() returns two outputs (priority, department), and the target structure must match exactly what call() returns.
questions.explanation: From the callout on the compile/fit code.

questions.question: What structure must the input data passed to fit() have here?
options: A list of three arrays in any order
A dict with keys title, text_body, tags
A single concatenated array of width 20100
questions.answer: A dict with keys title, text_body, tags
questions.explanation: call() reads inputs["title"], inputs["text_body"], inputs["tags"]. A list would fail on key access; concatenation happens inside the model; the tuple is the output.

questions.question: Which line in call() corresponds to the shared Dense(64) layer of the Functional model?
questions.explanation: mixing_layer is Dense(64, relu), defined on p.226.

questions.question: If call() returned department, priority (in that order), what would have to change in compile() and fit()?
questions.answer: The order of the losses, metrics and target arrays would have to be swapped to match the new return order.
questions.explanation: Pairing is by the structure of call()'s return value.

questions.question: Can you explain, using this page and p.223, why you can pass targets as a dict keyed by "priority" to the Functional model but the book uses a list for the subclassed one?
questions.answer: In the Functional model those are names of output layers; the subclassed model returns an unnamed pair, so the target structure is a two-element list.
